# Graph `example_graph`

## Is it available here?

If you have not yet in this session: `graph start --json` (it refreshes stale skills, lists the graphs and what your token may use of each, and how to search them).

Load the `graph-cli` skill as well before your first `graph` command: it has every command with its options, the change sets of `graph apply` and the error codes. The rules of working with `graph` below hold from the first call, with or without it.

Use this skill only if an item named `example_graph` is listed (title: Example graph) by `graph start` or `graph graphs --json`. Pass `--graph example_graph` to every command, as the examples here do, so they work in every directory; a project whose pointer makes `example_graph` the default may leave it out.

Text values are written in the graph language `en`.

Working with `graph`:

- Run each call as a plain command that starts with `graph` and passes `--json`: no `cd`, variables, loops, pipes or heredocs, which a restricted harness refuses. If a call is refused, run it again in that form before you give up.
- Read the answer: `ok`, then `data`; on failure `error.hint` is the command to run next. Never cut an answer short; ask for less: `--fields <attr>,<attr>` on `find`, `get` and `neighbors`, or `graph query` with `RETURN` of just the columns you need (`graph describe schema --compact --json` lists the patterns).
- For what is known about one entity, `graph view <id> --json` answers in one call (key fields, relations with counts, files, what applies next): use it before walking edges with `get` and `neighbors`.
- Never guess an option, type, field, relation or state: `graph <command> --help` lists the options, `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json` the fields, states and relations.
- For a question, run a named function when one fits (`graph run <function> --param <name>=<value>`); write a `graph query` only when none does. An empty value in a function's answer means nothing is recorded: say so instead of searching further.
- For a change, run a named action when one fits (`graph do <action> --param <name>=<value> --dry-run`, read what it will change, then run it without `--dry-run`). Otherwise preview `create`, `apply`, `transition`, `supersede` and `retract` with `--dry-run`, then run them without; one `update`, `link` or `unlink` may run directly. Say why in `--reason`, with how you learned it (in English, whatever language the values are in), never in a field value, and pass `--expect <rev>` when the write depends on what you read. A change set for `graph apply` goes into a file in the working directory.
- Before you create an entity with a name, look the name up (`graph lookup '<name>' --json`) and use the one that exists, never a second one under a similar name: the write finding `data.semantic.possible_duplicate` names near spellings, also on a dry run.
- Ask the user before `retract`.
- Read `data.findings` of every write and tell the user about each warning.

The graph stores files: `graph file add <file> --graph example_graph --json` stores one, and entities point to it with `files:from_file` and the page; the `graph-cli` skill section Files says how.

## What is in it

| Module | Prefix | What it holds | Types | Links to other modules |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `staff` | `stf` | Employees, contractors, crews, badges and personnel files. | 6 | none |

Built-in modules, shared by every graph: `core`, `files`.

- Before you work in a module, read it: `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph` lists its types, its relations, its links to and from other modules (with the other module named) and its rules. Read its text; `--json` is more than twice the size.
- To find a term whose module you do not know: `graph describe search <text> --graph example_graph --json` (types, relations, fields, enum values and states).
- For the fields, states and relations of one type: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
- The functions and actions of a module are listed by the same command, not here: `graph describe module <module> --graph example_graph`.

| Type | What it is | Fields | States |
|---|---|---|---|
| `files:File` (`FILE-0001`) | A file whose bytes the graph stores. | `title` (required, main name); `content` (blob, required, unique, write-once); `media_type` (required, write-once); `file_name` (write-once); `origin` (local_path); `retrieved_at` (date, write-once); `source_url` (iri, write-once) | none |
| `stf:Badge` (`BDG-0001`) | An access badge. | `holder_name` (main name, marked stf:personal); `number` (integer) | none |
| `stf:Contractor` (`CON-0001`) | A colleague hired through an agency. Is a `stf:Colleague`. | `name` (required, main name); `agency`; `email`; `phone` | none |
| `stf:Crew` (`CREW-0001`) | A group of colleagues working together. | `name` (required, main name) | none |
| `stf:Employee` (`EMP-0001`) | A colleague on the payroll. Is a `stf:Colleague`. | `name` (required, main name); `badge_code` (marked stf:personal); `birth_date` (date, marked stf:personal); `email` (marked stf:personal); `pay_grade` (one of `junior`, `senior`, marked stf:personal); `phone`; `shift` (one of `day`, `night`); `weekly_hours` (integer, marked stf:personal) | `stage`: `started` -> `equipped`, `started` -> `scheduled`; initial `started` |
| `stf:PersonnelFile` (`PF-0001`) | A stored document about a colleague. Is a `files:File`. | `title` (required, main name); `content` (blob, required, unique, write-once); `media_type` (required, write-once); `file_name` (write-once); `origin` (local_path); `remark` (marked stf:personal); `retrieved_at` (date, write-once); `source_url` (iri, write-once) | none |

Other types of the model, described in `references/model.md`: `files:FormatMetadata`, `files:Metadata`, `files:MetadataPart`, `stf:Colleague`.

Relations:

Each relation with its pattern for `graph query` (a label matches its subtypes too):

- `files:from_file` `()-[:from_file]->(:File)` (out 0..n, qualifiers `last_page`, `locator`, `page`): Information in the source entity was taken from the file.
- `files:metadata_of` `(:Metadata)-[:metadata_of]->(:File)` (out 1..1): The metadata record describes the file.
- `stf:concerns` `(:PersonnelFile)-[:concerns]->(:Colleague)` (out 0..n): The colleague a personnel file is about.
- `stf:holds_badge` `(:Employee)-[:holds_badge]->(:Badge)` (out 0..1): The badge an employee holds.
- `stf:in_crew` `(:Colleague)-[:in_crew]->(:Crew)` (out 0..1): The crew a colleague works in.

Constraints:

- `stf:Employee` `stage` `started` -> `equipped`: The badge code is recorded. (guard `stf.badge_known`)
- `stf:Employee` `stage` `started` -> `scheduled`: The shift is recorded. (guard `stf.shift_known`)
- Rule `stf.contractor_contact` on `stf:Contractor` (warning, checked on every write): A contractor with an e-mail names the agency.
- Rule `stf.crew_hours` on `stf:Crew` (warning, checked on every write): A crew works at most 400 hours a week.
- Rule `stf.employee_contact` on `stf:Employee` (warning, checked on every write): An employee with a private e-mail has a work phone.

## Names and ids

- Aliases such as `FILE-0001`: the type table names each type's. The number is zero-padded to 4 digits (`FILE-0001`, never `FILE-1`) and grows past 9999. A full id works everywhere; on the command line 8 or more trailing hex digits of it work too.
- `graph lookup <value> --graph example_graph --json` finds entities by name, ignoring case; it matches the fields the type table marks main name, other names, hidden names, not other text.
- Names are not unique, so `lookup` returns candidates; `--for <relation>` or `--for <function>.<param>` keeps those that can fill that slot. Use the returned alias or id only when exactly one candidate matches exactly (`match.kind` is `exact`). With several, or only prefix matches, do not answer about one of them first: unless type and `facts` show which one the request means, list them with their names and ask which one is meant, then answer.
- `graph search <value> --graph example_graph --json` searches names and every text field, forgiving case, accents, typos and parts of words. Its results are suggestions: read one with `graph get` before you use it.
- When you create an entity of a type with names: if `lookup` finds the same thing under another name, add the new name to its other names field instead of creating another; fill the other names fields of a new one with the abbreviations and synonyms people use.

## Model

Every type with all its fields, lifecycles, relations and rules: [references/model.md](references/model.md). The live source, which wins when they differ: `graph describe type <type> --graph example_graph --json`.
